title: A2 consolidation
objectives: I can tell a short story that mixes the preterite, the imperfect and the progressive, linked with connectors.
I can use connectors such as mas, porém, então, por isso, porque, quando and enquanto, and recognize embora.
I can solve everyday problems in shops and services by complaining, exchanging, cancelling and rescheduling politely.
I can write a short informal message and a short formal email with a clear greeting, purpose, request and closing.
I can explain why the words of this unit are spelled and accented as they are, and what embora and its subjunctive verb do.

vocabulary.note: Written-register equivalent of mas. It can also follow the first word of its clause: O hotel, porém, é caro. Spelling: po-RÉM is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in em, so it takes an acute accent.

example.pt: O hotel é bonito, porém muito caro.
example.en: The hotel is beautiful, but very expensive.

vocabulary.note: Formal and mostly written; speech prefers mas. Entanto is an old word for the time in between, and no is em plus o. The contrast arises because what happened in the meantime went against expectation.

example.pt: Estudei muito. No entanto, não passei na prova.
example.en: I studied a lot. However, I did not pass the test.
example.literal: I-studied a-lot. In-the meanwhile, not I-passed in-the test.

vocabulary.note: Adds a further point in the same direction. Disso is de plus isso. Spelling: a-LÉM is stressed on the last syllable, so it takes an acute accent, like também.

example.pt: O apartamento é barato. Além disso, fica perto do metrô.
example.en: The apartment is cheap. Besides, it is near the subway.
example.literal: The apartment is cheap. Beyond of-this, it-stays near of-the subway.

vocabulary.note: Isso points back at what was just said, so por isso introduces the result. The reason comes first and the result second.

example.pt: Choveu muito, por isso ficamos em casa.
example.en: It rained a lot, so we stayed home.
example.literal: It-rained a-lot, for this we-stayed in house.

vocabulary.note: Formal; in speech people say então or por isso. Spelling: por-TAN-to ends in o, so the stress on the second to last syllable is the default and no accent is written. The a is nasal because n follows it in its syllable.

example.pt: O voo atrasou, portanto vou chegar mais tarde.
example.en: The flight was delayed, therefore I will arrive later.

vocabulary.note: Seja is a form of the verb ser (the same word as in the command Seja pontual). The phrase restates what was just said.

example.pt: Ele chega às dez, ou seja, daqui a uma hora.
example.en: He arrives at ten, that is, in an hour.
example.literal: He arrives at-the ten, or it-be, from-here to an hour.

vocabulary.note: Says that something happened despite an obstacle. Spelling: the s of mesmo is said z because it comes before the voiced consonant m, and the ss of assim is always s.

example.pt: Estava chovendo, mas mesmo assim fomos à praia.
example.en: It was raining, but we went to the beach anyway.
example.literal: It-was raining, but even thus we-went to-the beach.

vocabulary.note: Followed by a noun, not by a clause with its own verb: por causa do trânsito (de plus o), por causa da chuva (de plus a). Before a clause with a verb, use porque. Spelling: trânsito is stressed on the third to last syllable, so it has an accent.

example.pt: Cheguei atrasado por causa do trânsito.
example.en: I arrived late because of the traffic.
example.literal: I-arrived late for cause of-the traffic.

vocabulary.note: The literal gloss is the historical origin, em boa hora. The same word is the adverb in ir embora, to leave. In standard Portuguese it is followed by the subjunctive: embora seja, embora esteja. Spelling: the em is nasal, written m before b.

example.pt: Embora seja caro, o hotel vale a pena.
example.en: Although it is expensive, the hotel is worth it.
example.literal: Although be expensive, the hotel is-worth the pain.

vocabulary.note: Adds an afterthought or a correction. It comes from Latin for otherwise. Spelling: a-li-ÁS is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for an ending in a plus s, so the acute accent is written.

example.pt: Aliás, você já viu o filme novo?
example.en: By the way, have you seen the new movie?

vocabulary.note: Reclamar de something (to complain about it), reclamar com someone (to complain to them). False friend: English reclaim is recuperar, not reclamar.

example.pt: Vou reclamar com o gerente do hotel.
example.en: I am going to complain to the hotel manager.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: the stem is troc-. Before an e a plain c would say s, so to keep the k sound the c becomes qu: troque, troquei.

example.pt: Posso trocar este tamanho por um maior?
example.en: Can I exchange this size for a bigger one?

vocabulary.note: Spelling: the first c is k before a, the second is s before e, which is the same rule seen from both sides.

example.pt: Preciso cancelar a minha reserva.
example.en: I need to cancel my reservation.

vocabulary.note: Marcar means to set a time or date (marcar uma consulta), and re- means again. The eu preterite is remarquei, with c changed to qu as in troquei.

example.pt: Podemos remarcar a reunião para quarta?
example.en: Can we reschedule the meeting for Wednesday?

vocabulary.note: Re- plus embolso, from bolsa, purse. The two e letters are two separate vowels in two syllables: re-em-BOL-so has four syllables.

example.pt: Quero pedir o reembolso do valor.
example.en: I want to ask for a refund of the amount.

vocabulary.note: Masculine although it ends in a, like o sistema and o programa: these words come from Greek nouns ending in -ma. Spelling: pro-BLE-ma is stressed on the second to last syllable, the default for an ending in a, and b and l stay together in one syllable.

example.pt: Qual é o problema?
example.en: What is the problem?

vocabulary.note: Also to sort out, to settle. Spelling: the s is between two vowels, so it says z (re-zol-VER), and the stress is on the last syllable because the ending is r.

example.pt: Vou resolver isso hoje.
example.en: I am going to sort this out today.

vocabulary.note: Portuguese often names a state with com plus a noun, as in estar com fome. Here the state is having a defect.

example.pt: O celular veio com defeito.
example.en: The phone came defective.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: ga-ran-TI-a is stressed on the i itself, which is the second to last syllable, so the default of the ending a applies and no accent is written. Compare tia.

example.pt: A garantia vale por um ano.
example.en: The warranty is valid for one year.
example.literal: The warranty is-worth for a year.

vocabulary.note: The official tax document issued with every sale; it works as the receipt and the proof of purchase for returns and warranty claims. Fiscal means relating to the tax authority. Spelling: fis-CAL, with s before c and final l said w.

example.pt: Guarde a nota fiscal para usar a garantia.
example.en: Keep the invoice to use the warranty.
example.literal: Keep the note fiscal for to-use the warranty.

vocabulary.note: Feminine like every noun in -ção; the plural is reclamações. Spelling: re-cla-ma-ÇÃO is stressed on the last syllable, as the ending ão predicts, and the cedilla keeps the s sound before a.

example.pt: Fiz uma reclamação no site da loja.
example.en: I filed a complaint on the store website.
example.literal: I-made a complaint in-the site of-the store.

vocabulary.note: Standard formal opening of a letter or email, from prezar, to value. Prezada for a woman, prezados for a group. The z is said z.

example.pt: Prezado senhor, escrevo para pedir informações.
example.en: Dear sir, I am writing to ask for information.

vocabulary.note: The usual closing of a formal email or letter. It is atenciosa, the feminine of atencioso, plus -mente, the ending that works like English -ly. Spelling: ten-ci-o-sa-MEN-te follows the default for an ending in e.

example.pt: Atenciosamente, Lucas Ferreira.
example.en: Sincerely, Lucas Ferreira.

vocabulary.en: I look forward to your reply
vocabulary.note: Business register. Aguardar is a formal word for to wait for, and retorno, return, is the business word for a reply. Spelling: in aguardo the gu is followed by a, so the u is sounded like a w: a-GWAR-du.

example.pt: Aguardo o seu retorno até sexta.
example.en: I look forward to your reply by Friday.
example.literal: I-await the your return until Friday.

vocabulary.note: Para plus an infinitive means in order to. Escrevendo is the gerund of escrever: an -er verb takes -endo.

example.pt: Estou escrevendo para pedir informações.
example.en: I am writing to ask for information.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: the x of anexo says ks, as in táxi. The e-mail convention is Segue em anexo, literally follows in attachment, with the attached thing as the subject of segue.

example.pt: Segue em anexo o comprovante de pagamento.
example.en: Attached is the proof of payment.
example.literal: Follows in attachment the proof of payment.

vocabulary.note: Friendly closing for messages to friends and colleagues; beijos, kisses, is warmer. Spelling: the cedilla gives the s sound before o.

example.pt: Até sábado! Um abraço.
example.en: See you Saturday! Best wishes.

vocabulary.note: Desculpe is the command form of desculpar, built as in the lesson on imperatives. Use it when a reply is late.

example.pt: Desculpe a demora, eu estava viajando.
example.en: Sorry for the delay, I was traveling.
example.literal: Excuse the delay, I was traveling.

vocabulary.note: Desde já means from now on. Spelling: the stem of agradecer is agradec-, and before -o a plain c would say k, so the cedilla keeps the s: agradeço.

example.pt: Agradeço desde já pela atenção.
example.en: Thank you in advance for your attention.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: stress and accents in this unit's words
grammar.explanation:
Every written accent in this unit's words comes from one rule, so this note applies the rule and adds nothing new. Recall it from the lesson on stress and accent marks. A word ending in a, e or o (with or without a final s), or in am, em or ens, is stressed on the second to last syllable. A word ending in anything else is stressed on the last syllable. A written accent appears only when a word breaks the default of its ending, and it sits on the stressed vowel. So an accent is a flag which says that this word is an exception to its ending, and no accent says that the default applies. The method is always the same: divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable by ear, read the default from the ending, and compare.

Stressed on the last syllable, although the ending predicts the second to last. Porém is po-RÉM. The ending em defaults to PO-rem, but the word is said on the last syllable, so an acute accent is required. Além (a-LÉM) and também (tam-BÉM) work in the same way, and aliás (a-li-ÁS) breaks the default of an ending in a plus s. Words ending in a, e or o behave alike: você (vo-CÊ), até (a-TÉ), metrô (me-TRÔ) and está (es-TÁ) are stressed on the last syllable although the ending predicts the second to last, so each is written with an accent; the shape follows the vowel, a circumflex for a closed e or o (você, metrô) and an acute for an open e or for a (até, está). Before m or n a vowel is nasal, so there is no open or closed vowel to hear in porém and além; there the accent only marks the stress. Compare portanto, por-TAN-to: the ending o already predicts the second to last syllable, so nothing is written. And compare então, en-TÃO: the ending ão defaults to the last syllable, so it breaks nothing, and the tilde is there only because the vowel is nasal.

Stressed on the third to last syllable. No ending predicts this, so the accent is always written: ônibus, trânsito, péssima, ótimo, número, áudio, formulário, sábado, sério. The mark is chosen by the vowel. The circumflex is used for a closed o (ônibus) and for a stressed a before m or n (trânsito, like câmera). The acute is used for an open vowel (péssima, ótimo) and for u (número), which has only one quality. In words that end in an unstressed i plus a vowel (-io, -ia), the i counts as its own syllable, so áudio is ÁU-di-o, sério is SÉ-ri-o and formulário is for-mu-LÁ-ri-o, all stressed on the third to last. Garantia looks similar but is different: ga-ran-TI-a is stressed on the i, which is second to last, so the default of the ending a already predicts it and nothing is written, just as in tia.

Stressed on the second to last, although the ending predicts the last. Difícil is di-FÍ-cil: the ending l defaults to the last syllable, the stress is one syllable earlier, so the accent is required. Táxi is TÁ-xi for the same reason with the ending i. Fácil and álbum are the same pattern.

One-syllable words and the hiatus. A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o takes an accent: dá, já, é, tá. The small unstressed word da (of the, from de plus a) has none; it is said quickly as part of the words around it, while dá carries the stress, so in writing the accent and the meaning tell them apart. In saí (I left) the a and the í are two separate syllables, sa-Í, which is called a hiatus; the stressed i is alone in its syllable, so it is marked. Sai (he leaves) is one syllable, with the diphthong ai, and needs no mark.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: letters and sound patterns in this unit
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese spelling is a code in which the letters next to a letter decide how it is said. The patterns below come from the lesson on sounds, and together they explain every unusual spelling in this unit. Each is a rule, not an exception to memorize.

The cedilla. The letter c says k before a, o and u, and s before e and i. To write the s sound before a, o or u, the c takes a cedilla: ç. That is why reclamação, abraço, agradeço and ligação are written as they are. It also explains verb forms. The stem of agradecer is agradec-, and the first person ending is -o, so a plain c would turn into k; the cedilla keeps the s, giving agradeço. The reverse problem gives troque. The stem of trocar is troc-, and before the ending -e a plain c would say s, so the c changes to qu, which says k before e. The ending -ção is the feminine noun ending (a reclamação, as reclamações), a nasal diphthong stressed on the last syllable.

The letters qu and gu. Before e or i the u is usually silent and only keeps the k sound or the hard g sound: quebrado, troque, segue. A few words sound it anyway (frequente, aguentar). Before a or o the u is a quick w: aguardo is a-GWAR-du and quando is KWAN-du. The vowel that follows tells you whether the u is silent or sounded: guarde is GWAR-ji, but ninguém is nin-GÉM. The same two spellings fix the first person of the past tense of verbs in -car and -gar. Before the ending -ei a plain c would say s and a plain g would say zh, so the sounds are kept with qu and gu: trocar gives troquei, explicar gives expliquei, chegar gives cheguei.

Nasal vowels. A vowel followed by m or n in the same syllable is said through the nose, and the m or n is not a separate consonant: em-BO-ra, en-TAN-to, por-TAN-to. Compare anexo, a-NE-ksu, where the n begins the second syllable and is a real consonant. The letter is m before b and p and n before other consonants. The tilde does the same job in ão and ões.

The letter s. At the start of a word it says s. A double ss always says s: disso, assim, péssima, assine. Between two vowels it says z: resolver is re-zol-VER, and trânsito is TRÂN-zi-tu (the s of the prefix trans- is also said z before a vowel). At the end of a syllable it depends on the next consonant. A voiced consonant is one said with the vocal cords vibrating (b, d, g, m, v, z, l, r, n), and before one the s says z: mesmo is MEZ-mu and desde is DEZ-ji. Before a voiceless consonant (p, t, c, f) the s says s: fiscal is fis-KAW. In Rio and some other regions this s is said like sh.

The letter x. It has several sounds and no single rule: ks in anexo and táxi, s in trouxe, sh in caixa, z in exemplo. The sound sh is more often spelled ch: chefe, preencha, chegou. Learn the sound of an x with the word.

Vowels that stay separate. In reembolso the prefix re- meets embolso, and the two e letters are two separate vowels in two syllables: re-em-BOL-so has four syllables. A double vowel is never a single long vowel: voo, flight, is vo-o, and since 2009 it is written without an accent, and reunião is re-u-ni-ÃO, where the e and u are also separate syllables.

Sounds that depend on position. In most of Brazil, t and d before the sound i (an i, or an unstressed final e) are said ch and j: desde ends in DEZ-ji, and atenciosamente ends in -MEN-chi. The final l is said w: fiscal is fis-KAW and hotel is o-TEW. The letter h is silent: hotel, hoje. The pair ou is one sound, a closed o followed by a w glide: ligou, quebrou, trouxe. The digraph nh is ny (cozinha, senhor), and j is always zh (janela).

grammar.title: Small words of conversation in the dialogues
grammar.explanation:
A fixed phrase is a group of words whose meaning belongs to the group and not to the words one by one. Every language has them: English says I am all ears and do not get me started, and nobody hears the ears or the starting. This course keeps three layers apart: what the words literally say, what an English speaker would say for the same purpose, and when the phrase is used. The dialogues of this unit contain several short fixed phrases, and the table gives all three layers.

Three mechanisms recur. First, interjections, which are words that express a feeling and have no grammar: puxa and nossa began as other words (the command puxa, pull, and the first word of Nossa Senhora, Our Lady) but are now only ways to show sympathy or surprise, and nobody hears pull or our. Second, a verb form used in a conventional way: pode deixar is literally can leave and means leave it to me, and nem me fale is literally not even me speak, using the command form fale, and means do not get me started. Third, an ordinary word moved into a new use: pessoal is an adjective meaning personal or relating to the staff, and became the noun for the people of a group, so Pessoal, ... addresses a group the way English says folks.

Two more patterns appear in the dialogues. Sim after a verb (Aviso, sim) is a plain confirmation of that verb, and answers a yes or no question by repeating the verb: I will. And não se esqueça de is the negative command of esquecer-se de, to forget to. It is a reflexive verb like the ones in the lesson on routines, so the pronoun se goes before the verb in the negative command. The cedilla of esqueça is the rule from the spelling note: the stem esquec- ends in a c, and before -a a plain c would say k.

grammar.title: Connectors: linking ideas
grammar.explanation:
A connector is a word or short phrase whose only job is to show how two statements relate. Without connectors a story is a list (I was tired. I went to bed.); with them it becomes an account (I was tired, so I went to bed). Portuguese and English draw the same relations: contrast (but, however), result (so, that is why), reason (because, because of), time (when, while), addition (besides), restating (in other words) and concession (although). What differs is four things: how formal the word is, which way the cause points, whether a noun or a whole clause (a group of words built around its own verb) follows, and whether the verb after it needs a special form. This note takes them in turn.

Contrast and register. Register is the level of formality of language. Mas is the everyday word for but; it sits between the two clauses and joins them: Gosto do hotel, mas é caro. Porém and no entanto express the same contrast in a more formal, mostly written register. Porém can also move inside its clause: O hotel, porém, é caro. Mesmo assim, literally even thus, is different: it does not join two clauses but says that something happened in spite of an obstacle just mentioned: Estava chovendo, mas mesmo assim fomos à praia. Além disso adds a further point in the same direction, and ou seja restates what was just said in other words, often to make it concrete.

Reason and result point in opposite directions, and the common mistake is to pick the word for the wrong direction. Porque introduces the reason, and the reason comes second: Fiquei em casa porque choveu. Então, por isso and portanto introduce the result, and the result comes second: Choveu, por isso fiquei em casa. Both sentences carry the same two facts in opposite order. The literal meanings explain the direction. Por isso is for this, pointing back at the sentence before it; porque is por (for) plus que (what); portanto is por plus tanto, for so much; and então is then. Portanto is formal, and in speech people say então or por isso.

Noun or clause. Porque needs a clause with its own verb. When the reason is only a noun, use por causa de, for cause of, which contracts with the article: por causa do trânsito (de plus o), por causa da chuva (de plus a). English makes the same split: because it rained is a clause, because of the rain is a noun.

Time. Quando links two moments and enquanto links two actions that overlap, and each one steers the tenses. Quando with the preterite names a completed event; with the imperfect it names a habit or a background: Quando eu era criança, morava em Recife. Enquanto means for as long as, from em plus quanto, in how much, so both actions are usually in the imperfect: Enquanto eu cozinhava, ele lia. If a sudden event happens during the overlap, that event takes the preterite: Enquanto eu esperava, começou a chover.

The four whys. They differ because of the stress rule, not by chance. Por que, two words, is por (for) plus que (what), used to ask a question: Por que você chegou tarde? Here que is unstressed, like any small word, so it has no accent. Porque, one word, is the conjunction because and answers the question: Porque perdi o ônibus. Por quê, with a circumflex, is used when the question ends the sentence: Você chegou tarde por quê? Now que is the last word and is stressed, and a stressed one-syllable word ending in e takes an accent, like pé. O porquê, one word with an accent, is the noun the reason: Não sei o porquê. It is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for an ending in e, so it is written with an accent. In an indirect question it is por que again: Não sei por que ele chegou tarde.

Embora means although, and it is the one connector that changes the verb: it requires a verb form called the subjunctive, which the next note explains.

grammar.title: Embora and the subjunctive: a first look
grammar.explanation:
A mood is the way a verb form presents what the sentence says (the grammar map introduced the term). The indicative presents it as a fact. The subjunctive presents it as something that is not being asserted at this moment: wished, doubted, not yet real or, as with embora, granted but not the point. In Embora seja caro, o hotel vale a pena, the price is not in doubt; the speaker grants it and moves on to the main claim. Portuguese marks that stance by switching the verb into the subjunctive.

English has a weak version of the same idea. In if I were you, the form were is a subjunctive, and it is not the form that goes with I in a statement of fact. Portuguese uses the subjunctive far more often, and the rule is mechanical: certain words always require it, and embora is one of them. In standard Portuguese the indicative is not used after embora, however certain the fact is. So the first job is to recognize the word and the verb form that follows it.

You already know many of the forms. The present subjunctive is built from the eu form of the present by dropping the -o and switching the vowel: -ar verbs take -e and -er and -ir verbs take -a. That is exactly the recipe for the command forms with você in the lesson on imperatives, so fale, coma and abra are the forms you already know, and so are the irregular ones seja, esteja, vá, dê and saiba. With embora the form is the one for ele, ela and você: embora seja, embora esteja, embora tenha, embora faça. Ou seja in the vocabulary is the same seja, which is why it literally says or it be.

For a situation that was true in the past Portuguese uses another subjunctive tense, the imperfect subjunctive: Embora fosse tarde, ficamos, although it was late, we stayed. Fosse is the form from se eu fosse você, if I were you. You are not asked to produce these yet. At this stage learn the whole phrases embora seja, embora esteja, embora tenha, embora faça and se eu fosse você, and recognize that the verb after embora looks different from the plain present.

Embora and mas express much the same contrast with different grammar. The embora clause is subordinate and takes the subjunctive; with mas the two clauses are independent and both take the indicative: Embora seja caro, vale a pena, or É caro, mas vale a pena. The embora clause can also come second: Vale a pena, embora seja caro. The same word is also the adverb in ir embora, to leave.

grammar.title: Review: telling a story and the A2 toolkit
grammar.explanation:
The two past tenses are not past and more past; they are two ways of looking at a past event, which is called aspect. The preterite is the view from outside: the event is a completed whole with an edge. The imperfect is the view from inside: the action was going on, was a habit or formed the scene. English uses several devices for the inside view (was playing, used to play, would play), while Portuguese has one tense and one question to ask of every verb: did this move the story forward, or does it describe the stage? Events that move the story forward take the preterite; the stage, meaning the time, the weather, the feelings and what else was going on, takes the imperfect.

A story therefore has three parts. The setting is in the imperfect: Eram oito horas, chovia, eu estava indo para o trabalho. The trigger is a sudden event in the preterite: de repente, o ônibus quebrou. The result is one or more preterite actions in order: liguei para o chefe, peguei um táxi. The classic pair is estava plus the gerund (the -ndo form that works like English -ing) for the ongoing action and the preterite for what interrupts it, joined by quando: Eu estava dormindo quando o telefone tocou. Enquanto joins two ongoing actions, both in the imperfect. Because the preterite and the imperfect are different questions, you can place both in one sentence: Eu estava cansado, então dormi cedo.

The rest of the A2 toolkit supplies the other parts of a story. Comparatives and superlatives give opinions: foi o pior dia da semana. Object pronouns go before the verb in speech: ele me ligou. Commands give advice, using the subjunctive-based forms for você: mande uma mensagem. Ir plus an infinitive or the simple future says what comes next: vou pedir desculpas. The irregular preterites (fui, fiz, trouxe, disse) must be known by heart, because they are the verbs of events. Verbs and prepositions do not always match English: esperar o ônibus is literally to wait the bus, with no equivalent of for, and responder takes an indirect object, so the pronoun is me or lhe (Ninguém me respondeu).

grammar.title: Common A2 errors
grammar.explanation:
Most mistakes at this level have one of two causes: translating English structure word for word, or applying a regular pattern to a word that does not follow it. Knowing which cause is at work is what lets you correct yourself. The table collects eight errors with the rule each one breaks.

Tense choice (English structure). The imperfect is for habits and background, the preterite for a sudden or completed event. English hides the difference, so say it to yourself in Portuguese terms: a habit in the past, Quando eu era criança, eu ia à praia, needs the imperfect; a sudden event, De repente, o telefone tocou, needs the preterite. A habit needs the imperfect because it has no edge to complete, and a sudden event needs the preterite because it does.

Irregular preterites (a regular pattern applied to an irregular word). Fiz, trouxe, soube and disse are common old verbs that keep irregular stems and do not take the regular endings, such as -ei for eu. Forms like fazi, trazi, sabi and dizi do not exist; learn the irregular ones as vocabulary.

Pronouns. After a preposition the form is mim, but when the pronoun is the subject of an infinitive it is eu, because the pronoun is performing a verb: Ele trouxe o livro para eu ler, where eu is the one who reads. Mim stays where no verb follows: Isso é para mim. In speech a short object pronoun goes before the verb (Ele me ligou); the written form with a hyphen after the verb (Ele ligou-me) is formal or European.

Gender, number and the verb to be. Nouns in -ma such as problema, sistema, programa and tema are masculine, because they come from Greek, and a foto and a mão are feminine although they end in o. Plurals in -ão vary (mãos, pães, limões), and -l changes to -is (animal, animais). Finally, Portuguese says many states with estar com or ter where English says to be: estar com fome is literally to be with hunger, and ter vinte anos is literally to have twenty years. And the progressive in Brazil is estou trabalhando, never estou a trabalhar.

grammar.title: Writing short messages and emails
grammar.explanation:
Writing in Portuguese follows the same principle as speaking: you choose the form for the relationship. A short message has four parts: a greeting, a reason for writing, a request or piece of information, and a closing. For a friend, keep it short and warm: Oi, Ana! Tudo bem? Estou escrevendo para avisar que vou atrasar. Me manda a localização? Um abraço! In messaging apps, abbreviations such as vc for você, pq for porque or por que, and tb for também are common among friends but are avoided at work.

For a formal email the same four parts use fixed formulas, and the literal meaning of each shows why it works. Prezado (prized) or Prezada, plus the person's title and name, opens the letter, or just Bom dia. Estou escrevendo para (I am writing for) states the purpose. A request is made with the conditional, as in the lesson on politeness, because the conditional softens a request: Você poderia me enviar... is gentler than Você pode me mandar..., and Gostaria de (I would like of) is gentler than Quero. Segue em anexo (follows in attachment) introduces an attachment. Agradeço desde já (I thank since already) thanks the reader in advance, Aguardo o seu retorno (I await your return) asks for a reply, and Atenciosamente (attentively) closes. In very formal writing o senhor or a senhora replaces você.

Use short sentences, connectors such as mas, além disso and por isso to link ideas, and a date or deadline when you need an answer. Reread the message before sending it, especially for accents and for the forms of você and o senhor. Because the spelling is a code, a missing accent changes the stress and sometimes the word: dá and da, saí and sai, pode and pôde.

culture.title: Complaints, consumer rights and tone
culture.text:
Brazilians usually begin a complaint politely. Even when the problem is serious, people start with Boa tarde, tudo bem? and explain calmly before asking for a solution; raising the voice at the person at the counter is considered rude and usually makes the exchange slower. The two documents that matter in a shop are the nota fiscal, the tax invoice that works as the receipt, and the garantia, the warranty. Keep the nota fiscal: without it a return is difficult.

Consumer protection in Brazil is strong on paper. The Código de Defesa do Consumidor, the Consumer Defense Code, is the national law, and Procon, short for Proteção e Defesa do Consumidor, is the public agency where customers can file a complaint about a product or service. For purchases made online or by phone, the law gives the customer seven days to change their mind and get a refund, the direito de arrependimento, literally the right of regret.

Most companies run a customer service line called the SAC, short for Serviço de Atendimento ao Consumidor, and many customers also post public complaints on websites and social media, where a quick reply from the company is common. In writing, the tone changes with the reader: Oi, tudo bem? for a friend, and Prezado senhor or Prezada senhora plus Atenciosamente for a company or a boss. A message to a friend might end with Um abraço or Beijos, while an email to a company ends with Atenciosamente and your full name.

Dá is a longer word
The accent shows that dá is feminine
exercises.explanation: A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o takes an accent (dá, já, é). Small unstressed words such as da, de and que take none.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of the word meaning hard or difficult?
choices: dificil
difícil
dificíl
dífícil
exercises.explanation: Di-FÍ-cil is stressed on the second to last syllable, but the ending l predicts the last syllable, so the stressed vowel takes an acute accent.

exercises.prompt: Where is the stress in garantia?
choices: ga-RAN-ti-a
GA-ran-ti-a
ga-ran-TI-a
ga-ran-ti-A
exercises.explanation: The ending a predicts the second to last syllable, which is the ti. The word is said that way, so it breaks no default and needs no accent.

exercises.prompt: Why does agradeço have a cedilla?
choices: Before o a plain c would say k, and the s sound is needed
To show that the stress is on the last syllable
To make the vowel nasal
Because it is a formal word
exercises.explanation: C says k before a, o and u. The stem agradec- ends in the s sound, so before the ending -o it needs the cedilla to keep that sound.

exercises.prompt: How is the gu of aguardo pronounced?
choices: Hard g with a silent u, as in segue
Like the j of janela
A g followed by a w glide: a-GWAR-do
Like gu in guitarra
exercises.explanation: Before e or i the u of gu is silent; before a or o it is sounded like a quick w, as the u of qu in quando.

exercises.prompt: How do you say Why did you arrive late?
choices: Por que você chegou tarde?
Porque você chegou tarde?
Porquê você chegou tarde?
Por quê você chegou tarde?
exercises.explanation: At the start of a question, por que is two words and que is unstressed, so it has no accent. Porque answers the question, and por quê is used at the end of a question.
At the end of a question que is stressed, and a stressed one-syllable word ending in e takes an accent: quê.

exercises.hint_en: I stayed home because it rained.
exercises.explanation: Porque introduces a reason, and a reason clause has its own verb (choveu).

exercises.hint_en: We arrived late because of the traffic.
exercises.explanation: A noun follows, so por causa de is used, and de contracts with the article o: por causa do.

exercises.prompt: Choose the best connector: Estava chovendo, ___ eu fiquei em casa.
choices: embora
porque
por isso
exercises.explanation: Por isso points back at the first clause and introduces the result. The reason comes first and the result second. Porque would reverse the direction.

exercises.hint_en: I was tired, so I went to sleep early.
exercises.explanation: Então, por isso and portanto introduce a result; the tiredness is the reason, so the connector points forward to the result.

exercises.prompt: Which form completes Embora o hotel ___ caro, eu gosto dele?
choices: é
seja
foi
exercises.explanation: Embora always requires the subjunctive. Seja is the subjunctive of ser, the form you know from the command Seja pontual.

exercises.prompt_pt: Embora ela ___ cansada, ela vai à aula.
exercises.hint_en: Although she is tired, she is going to class.
exercises.explanation: Embora requires the subjunctive, and the subjunctive of estar is esteja, the same form as in the command Esteja aqui às oito.

exercises.audio_pt: Choveu muito, por isso ficamos em casa.
choices: It rained a lot, because we stayed home.
It rained a little, so we went out.
It rained a lot, so we stayed home.

exercises.audio_pt: Comprei o produto, mas ele chegou com defeito.
choices: I sold the product, but it arrived late.
I bought the product, but it arrived defective.
I bought the product, and it arrived early.

exercises.audio_pt: Quero cancelar a compra e receber o reembolso.
choices: I want to cancel the purchase and receive a refund.
I want to confirm the purchase and receive the receipt.
I want to repeat the purchase and receive a gift.

exercises.audio_pt: Enquanto eu esperava, a ligação caiu.
choices: After I waited, I hung up.
While I was talking, he was waiting.
While I was waiting, the call dropped.

exercises.prompt: Why are both verbs in the imperfect in Enquanto eu cozinhava, ele lia?
choices: Both actions were in progress at the same time, so both are background
The imperfect is always used after enquanto, even for one completed event
Both actions are finished and completed
exercises.explanation: Enquanto links two overlapping actions, each seen from the inside. If a sudden event happened during them, that event would take the preterite.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly combines an ongoing action and an interruption?
choices: Eu dormi quando o telefone tocava.
Eu estava dormindo quando o telefone tocou.
Eu estive dormindo quando o telefone tocou.
exercises.explanation: The ongoing action is the scene, so it takes the imperfect (estava dormindo); the interruption is an event with an edge, so it takes the preterite.

exercises.prompt_pt: Ontem eu ___ o jantar para todo mundo.
exercises.hint_en: Yesterday I made dinner for everybody.
exercises.explanation: Fiz is the irregular preterite of fazer. The regular form fazi does not exist.

exercises.prompt_pt: Enquanto eu ___ o jantar, ele arrumava a casa.
exercises.hint_en: While I made dinner, he tidied the house.
exercises.explanation: Two ongoing actions at the same time take the imperfect.

exercises.prompt_pt: Gosto do apartamento, ___ ele é caro demais.
exercises.hint_en: I like the apartment, but it is too expensive.
exercises.explanation: Mas and porém introduce a contrast; porém and no entanto are more formal.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses the correct gender for problema?
choices: A problema é grande.
O problema é grande.
Os problema é grande.
exercises.explanation: Problema is masculine, like sistema and programa: nouns in -ma from Greek are masculine. The plural needs os problemas.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses the pronoun correctly: He brought the book for me to read?
choices: Ele trouxe o livro para mim ler.
Ele trouxe o livro para me ler.
Ele trouxe o livro para eu ler.
exercises.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of the infinitive ler, so it is eu. Mim is used only when no verb follows the pronoun.

exercises.prompt_pt: Essa ajuda é muito importante para ___.
exercises.hint_en: This help is very important for me.
exercises.explanation: No verb follows the pronoun, so after a preposition the form is mim.

exercises.prompt: Which request is the most polite in a formal email?
choices: Me manda o comprovante.
Você pode mandar o comprovante?
Você poderia me enviar o comprovante?
exercises.explanation: The conditional (poderia) softens a request, and enviar is a little more formal than mandar.

exercises.prompt: Pode deixar is literally can leave. What is it used for?
choices: To reassure someone: leave it to me, I will handle it
To ask someone to leave
To apologize for a mistake
exercises.explanation: The literal gloss and the use differ: the phrase is a stock reassurance, as in English leave it to me.

exercises.prompt_en: I bought the phone, but it arrived broken.
That is why I am writing to you.
While I was sleeping, the phone rang.
Although it is expensive, it is worth it.
I was tired, but I went to the party.
answers: Eu estava cansado, mas fui à festa.
Estava cansado, mas fui à festa.
Eu estava cansada, mas fui à festa.
Estava cansada, mas fui à festa.
Eu estava cansado, mas fui para a festa.
Estava cansado, mas fui para a festa.
Eu estava cansada, mas fui para a festa.
Estava cansada, mas fui para a festa.
Eu estava cansado, mas fui pra festa.
Estava cansado, mas fui pra festa.
Eu estava cansada, mas fui pra festa.
Estava cansada, mas fui pra festa.
exercises.explanation: Tiredness is the background (imperfect), going to the party is the event (preterite).

exercises.prompt_en: I would like to exchange this product.
answers: Gostaria de trocar este produto.
Gostaria de trocar esse produto.
Eu gostaria de trocar este produto.
Eu gostaria de trocar esse produto.
Queria trocar este produto.
Queria trocar esse produto.
Eu queria trocar este produto.
Eu queria trocar esse produto.
exercises.explanation: Gostaria de is the conditional, literally I would like of; queria is the polite imperfect.

exercises.prompt_en: While I was working, my brother called me.
answers: Enquanto eu trabalhava, meu irmão me ligou.
Enquanto eu estava trabalhando, meu irmão me ligou.
Enquanto trabalhava, meu irmão me ligou.
Enquanto eu trabalhava, o meu irmão me ligou.
Enquanto eu trabalhava, meu irmão ligou pra mim.
Enquanto eu trabalhava, meu irmão ligou para mim.
exercises.explanation: The ongoing action is in the imperfect and the call is a preterite event; the pronoun me goes before the verb.

exercises.prompt_en: Although it is expensive, I bought it.
answers: Embora seja caro, eu comprei.
Embora seja caro, comprei.
Embora seja caro, eu comprei isso.
Embora seja caro, comprei isso.
Embora seja caro, eu comprei ele.
Embora seja caro, comprei ele.
Embora seja caro, eu o comprei.
Embora seja caro, comprei-o.
Embora seja cara, eu comprei.
Embora seja cara, comprei.
exercises.explanation: Embora requires the subjunctive seja; the main clause is a completed event in the preterite.

exercises.prompt_en: I arrived late because of the traffic.
answers: Cheguei atrasado por causa do trânsito.
Eu cheguei atrasado por causa do trânsito.
Cheguei atrasada por causa do trânsito.
Eu cheguei atrasada por causa do trânsito.
Cheguei tarde por causa do trânsito.
Eu cheguei tarde por causa do trânsito.
exercises.explanation: A noun follows, so por causa de contracts with the article: por causa do trânsito.

exercises.audio_pt: Prezado senhor, estou escrevendo para reclamar.
exercises.hint_en: Dear sir, I am writing to complain.
Thank you in advance for your attention.

exercises.audio_pt: Segue em anexo a nota fiscal.
Agradeço desde já e aguardo o seu retorno.
exercises.hint_en: Thank you in advance, and I look forward to your reply.
